#!/usr/bin/env bash
# compare-local.sh — start a ForgeMark comparison run (GitHub vs Entire) on the
# local `forgemark serve` GUI without any token handling at all: targets are
# posted with a secret_source ("gh" | "entire") and the SERVER pulls each
# credential from your already-authenticated CLI at run start. No token ever
# passes through this script, the request body, or the browser.
#
# One-time setup: scripts/login.sh (authenticates both CLIs). Everything else
# is automatic — the throwaway GitHub repo, its EntireDB mirror (or a native
# EntireDB repo), and the local server itself are created or started on first
# use. Entire endpoints come from the server's own discovery endpoint
# (GET /api/local/suggest), so that logic lives in exactly one place.
#
# Usage: scripts/compare-local.sh
#
# Overridable via environment variables:
#   FM_ADDR                 server address            (default 127.0.0.1:8377)
#   FM_GH_REPO              GitHub throwaway repo     (default <you>/forgemark-target, auto-created private)
#   FM_GITHUB_ONLY          set to 1 to skip the Entire target
#   FM_ENTIRE_NATIVE        set to 1 to benchmark a NATIVE EntireDB repo
#                           (et/<project>/<repo>, auto-created) instead of a
#                           GitHub mirror. A mirror write-throughs to GitHub on
#                           every push, so mirror mode measures the sync flow;
#                           native mode measures EntireDB itself.
#   FM_ENTIRE_PROJECT       native mode: owning project (default forgemark-<you>, auto-created)
#   FM_ENTIRE_REPO_NAME     native mode: repo name (default forgemark-target, auto-created)
#   FM_ENTIRE_UPSTREAM      mirror mode: GitHub repo behind the mirror (default
#                           <you>/forgemark-target-entire, auto-created private).
#                           Deliberately NOT the same repo as FM_GH_REPO: the
#                           mirror writes through to its GitHub upstream, so
#                           sharing one repo makes the two targets race each
#                           other's refs ("mirror is stale" on every push).
#   FM_ENTIRE_CLUSTER       EntireDB cluster host     (default: from /api/local/suggest)
#   FM_ENTIRE_REPOS         Entire repo path(s)       (default: the auto-created mirror/native repo)
#   FM_ENTIRE_NAME          chart label               (default: from /api/local/suggest, e.g. entire-in)
#   FM_ENTIRE_TOKEN_URL     core /oauth/token         (default: from /api/local/suggest)
#   FM_ENTIRE_JURISDICTION  jurisdiction audience     (default: from /api/local/suggest)
#   FM_CONCURRENCY          sweep, comma-separated    (default 1,4 — github.com abuse limits)
#   FM_DURATION_SEC         seconds per level         (default 30)
#   FM_WARMUP_SEC           warm-up seconds           (default 5)
#   FM_FILES_MIN/FM_FILES_MAX/FM_FILE_SIZE  commit shape (defaults 1/10/2048)
#   FM_VIEW                 UI view to open           (run | race, default run)
set -euo pipefail

ADDR="${FM_ADDR:-127.0.0.1:8377}"
CONCURRENCY="${FM_CONCURRENCY:-1,4}"
DURATION_SEC="${FM_DURATION_SEC:-30}"
WARMUP_SEC="${FM_WARMUP_SEC:-5}"

command -v gh >/dev/null || { echo "compare-local: needs the gh CLI — run scripts/login.sh" >&2; exit 1; }
command -v python3 >/dev/null || { echo "compare-local: needs python3" >&2; exit 1; }
gh auth status >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "compare-local: gh is not authenticated — run scripts/login.sh" >&2; exit 1; }

# --- server: start one if nothing is listening (needed before discovery) ---
if ! curl -sf "http://$ADDR/api/runs" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "compare-local: no server on $ADDR — starting one (logs: /tmp/forgemark-serve.log)"
  if command -v forgemark >/dev/null; then
    nohup forgemark serve -addr "$ADDR" >/tmp/forgemark-serve.log 2>&1 &
  else
    nohup go run ./cmd/forgemark serve -addr "$ADDR" >/tmp/forgemark-serve.log 2>&1 &
  fi
  for _ in $(seq 1 30); do
    curl -sf "http://$ADDR/api/runs" >/dev/null 2>&1 && break
    sleep 1
  done
  curl -sf "http://$ADDR/api/runs" >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "compare-local: server did not come up; see /tmp/forgemark-serve.log" >&2; exit 1; }
fi

# ensure_repo <owner/repo>: throwaway private repo with an initial commit
# (the EntireDB mirror's initial clone needs one), created on first use.
ensure_repo() {
  local repo="$1"
  if ! gh repo view "$repo" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    echo "compare-local: creating throwaway private repo $repo"
    gh repo create "$repo" --private --add-readme
  elif ! gh api "repos/$repo/commits?per_page=1" --jq '.[0].sha' >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    echo "compare-local: seeding empty repo $repo with an initial commit"
    gh api -X PUT "repos/$repo/contents/README.md" \
      -f message="forgemark bench target" \
      -f content="$(printf 'forgemark bench target\n' | base64)" >/dev/null
  fi
}

# --- GitHub target ---
GH_USER="$(gh api user --jq .login)"
GH_REPO="${FM_GH_REPO:-$GH_USER/forgemark-target}"
ensure_repo "$GH_REPO"
export GH_REPO

# --- Entire target: endpoints from the server's discovery, repo provisioned here ---
ENTIRE_ENABLED=0
if [ "${FM_GITHUB_ONLY:-0}" != "1" ]; then
  command -v entire >/dev/null || { echo "compare-local: entire CLI not found — run scripts/login.sh (or FM_GITHUB_ONLY=1)" >&2; exit 1; }
  entire auth status >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "compare-local: entire is not authenticated — run scripts/login.sh (or FM_GITHUB_ONLY=1)" >&2; exit 1; }

  # One discovery source: the same /api/local/suggest the GUI's "Add from CLI
  # logins" button uses. It runs gh+entire discovery server-side in parallel.
  SUGGEST="$(curl -sf "http://$ADDR/api/local/suggest")" \
    || { echo "compare-local: GET /api/local/suggest failed" >&2; exit 1; }
  export SUGGEST
  eval "$(python3 - <<'PY'
import json, os, shlex, sys

entry = json.loads(os.environ["SUGGEST"]).get("entire") or {}
if entry.get("error") or not entry.get("target"):
    print(f'echo "compare-local: entire discovery failed: {shlex.quote(entry.get("error", "no target"))}" >&2; exit 1')
    sys.exit(0)
t = entry["target"]
repo = (t.get("repos") or [""])[0]          # et/forgemark-<handle>/forgemark-target
jur = t.get("jurisdiction", "")             # https://<slug>.entire.io
slug = jur.removeprefix("https://").split(".")[0]
print(f'SUG_NAME={shlex.quote(t.get("name", ""))}')
print(f'SUG_REMOTE={shlex.quote(t.get("remote", ""))}')
print(f'SUG_TOKEN_URL={shlex.quote(t.get("token_url", ""))}')
print(f'SUG_JURISDICTION={shlex.quote(jur)}')
print(f'SUG_SLUG={shlex.quote(slug)}')
print(f'SUG_NATIVE_REPO={shlex.quote(repo)}')
PY
)"

  export FM_ENTIRE_NAME="${FM_ENTIRE_NAME:-$SUG_NAME}"
  export FM_ENTIRE_REMOTE="${FM_ENTIRE_REMOTE:-$SUG_REMOTE}"
  export FM_ENTIRE_TOKEN_URL="${FM_ENTIRE_TOKEN_URL:-$SUG_TOKEN_URL}"
  export FM_ENTIRE_JURISDICTION="${FM_ENTIRE_JURISDICTION:-$SUG_JURISDICTION}"
  ENTIRE_CLUSTER="${FM_ENTIRE_CLUSTER:-${FM_ENTIRE_REMOTE#https://}}"

  if [ "${FM_ENTIRE_NATIVE:-0}" = "1" ]; then
    # Native EntireDB repo: no GitHub in the write path. The suggest endpoint
    # already names the per-user default (project names are deployment-global).
    ENTIRE_REPO_PATH="${FM_ENTIRE_REPOS:-$SUG_NATIVE_REPO}"
    if [ -z "${FM_ENTIRE_PROJECT:-}" ] && [ -z "${FM_ENTIRE_REPO_NAME:-}" ]; then
      ENTIRE_PROJECT="$(cut -d/ -f2 <<<"$ENTIRE_REPO_PATH")"
      ENTIRE_REPO_NAME="$(cut -d/ -f3 <<<"$ENTIRE_REPO_PATH")"
    else
      ENTIRE_PROJECT="${FM_ENTIRE_PROJECT:-forgemark-$GH_USER}"
      ENTIRE_REPO_NAME="${FM_ENTIRE_REPO_NAME:-forgemark-target}"
      ENTIRE_REPO_PATH="et/$ENTIRE_PROJECT/$ENTIRE_REPO_NAME"
    fi
    if ! entire repo list "$ENTIRE_PROJECT" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
      ENTIRE_HANDLE="$(entire auth status | awk '/User:/{sub(/^@/, "", $2); print $2}')"
      echo "compare-local: creating project $ENTIRE_PROJECT (region $SUG_SLUG)"
      entire project create "$ENTIRE_PROJECT" --owner "github:$ENTIRE_HANDLE" --owner-type account --region "$SUG_SLUG"
    fi
    if ! entire repo get "$ENTIRE_REPO_NAME" --project "$ENTIRE_PROJECT" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
      echo "compare-local: creating native repo $ENTIRE_PROJECT/$ENTIRE_REPO_NAME on $ENTIRE_CLUSTER"
      entire repo create "$ENTIRE_REPO_NAME" --project "$ENTIRE_PROJECT" --cluster-host "$ENTIRE_CLUSTER"
    fi
  else
    # Mirror mode: own upstream per target (see FM_ENTIRE_UPSTREAM above).
    # Mirror create is idempotent on (upstream, cluster) and waits for the
    # initial GitHub→EntireDB clone so the first push has a repo to land in.
    ENTIRE_UPSTREAM="${FM_ENTIRE_UPSTREAM:-$GH_USER/forgemark-target-entire}"
    ensure_repo "$ENTIRE_UPSTREAM"
    echo "compare-local: ensuring mirror of $ENTIRE_UPSTREAM on $ENTIRE_CLUSTER"
    entire repo mirror create "https://github.com/$ENTIRE_UPSTREAM" "$ENTIRE_CLUSTER"
    ENTIRE_REPO_PATH="gh/$ENTIRE_UPSTREAM"
  fi
  export FM_ENTIRE_REPOS="${FM_ENTIRE_REPOS:-$ENTIRE_REPO_PATH}"
  ENTIRE_ENABLED=1
fi

# Targets carry secret_source, never a secret: the server execs `gh auth
# token` / `entire auth token` itself at run start.
export ENTIRE_ENABLED CONCURRENCY DURATION_SEC WARMUP_SEC
BODY="$(python3 - <<'PY'
import json, os

def opt_int(workload, key, env):
    v = os.environ.get(env)
    if v:
        workload[key] = int(v)

targets = [{
    "name": "github",
    "remote": "https://github.com",
    "repos": [os.environ["GH_REPO"]],
    "secret_source": "gh",
}]
if os.environ["ENTIRE_ENABLED"] == "1":
    targets.append({
        "name": os.environ["FM_ENTIRE_NAME"],
        "remote": os.environ["FM_ENTIRE_REMOTE"],
        "repos": [r for r in os.environ["FM_ENTIRE_REPOS"].split(",") if r],
        "secret_source": "entire",
        "token_url": os.environ["FM_ENTIRE_TOKEN_URL"],
        "jurisdiction": os.environ["FM_ENTIRE_JURISDICTION"],
    })

workload = {
    "strategy": "branch",
    "branch_prefix": "bench/",
    "concurrency": [int(c) for c in os.environ["CONCURRENCY"].split(",")],
    "duration_sec": float(os.environ["DURATION_SEC"]),
    "warmup_sec": float(os.environ["WARMUP_SEC"]),
}
opt_int(workload, "files_min", "FM_FILES_MIN")
opt_int(workload, "files_max", "FM_FILES_MAX")
opt_int(workload, "file_size", "FM_FILE_SIZE")

print(json.dumps({
    "confirm_authorized": True,  # your repos on both sides — see the README warning
    "workload": workload,
    "targets": targets,
}))
PY
)"

# One POST, body and status captured together: a retry-to-print-the-error
# would itself start a benchmark run.
HTTP_RESP="$(curl -s -w $'\n%{http_code}' -X POST "http://$ADDR/api/runs" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-binary @- <<<"$BODY")"
CODE="${HTTP_RESP##*$'\n'}"
RESP="${HTTP_RESP%$'\n'*}"
if [ "$CODE" != "201" ]; then
  echo "compare-local: starting the run failed (HTTP $CODE): $RESP" >&2
  exit 1
fi

RUN_ID="$(python3 -c 'import json,sys; d=json.loads(sys.argv[1]); print(d["id"])' "$RESP")"
python3 -c 'import json,sys; [print("compare-local: warning:", w) for w in json.loads(sys.argv[1]).get("warnings") or []]' "$RESP"

URL="http://$ADDR/#${FM_VIEW:-run}/$RUN_ID"
echo "compare-local: run $RUN_ID started — $URL"
command -v open >/dev/null && open "$URL" || true

# login.sh — authenticate the two CLIs that scripts/compare-local.sh depends
# on: gh (GitHub) and entire (EntireDB). Idempotent: already-valid logins are
# left alone, missing ones launch the CLI's own interactive login flow.
set -euo pipefail

command -v gh >/dev/null || { echo "login: gh CLI not found — install it from https://cli.github.com" >&2; exit 1; }
command -v entire >/dev/null || { echo "login: entire CLI not found — install it from https://docs.entire.io" >&2; exit 1; }

if gh auth status >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "login: gh — already authenticated as $(gh api user --jq .login)"
else
  echo "login: gh — not authenticated, starting gh auth login"
  gh auth login
fi

if entire auth status >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "login: entire — already authenticated ($(entire auth status | awk '/User:/{print $2}') on $(entire auth status | awk '/Context:/{print $2}'))"
else
  echo "login: entire — not authenticated, starting entire login"
  entire login
fi

echo "login: both CLIs ready — run scripts/compare-local.sh"

content.text:
All 19 findings are fixed and verified — full test suite green, JS syntax-checked, and every fix exercised live.

**The 10 primary findings:**

1. **Wildcard bind warning** — `IsLoopbackHost` is now exported from the server package (deduping the two copies) and treats an empty host as non-loopback. Verified live: `forgemark serve -addr :9999` now prints the warning.
2. **Script re-POST on failure** — one curl captures body and status together (`-w '\n%{http_code}'`); the error path prints what it already has instead of firing a second run-starting request.
3. **Silent 128-agent sweep** — two layers: newrun.js rejects malformed concurrency with an error banner before POSTing, and `withDefaults` only defaults a *nil* concurrency, so an explicit `[]` now 400s ("no concurrency levels" — verified via curl).
4. **clone_depth 0 unrepresentable** — fixed by the pointer rework below; explicit 0 passes through as full-history, and a new `Validate` check rejects negatives.
5. **Demo targets under clone/session** — `demoRunner.opFor()` emits `OpClone` for clone strategy and a clone-per-session for session. Verified: a demo clone run now reports real numbers (935 clones @ 77.9/s) instead of zeros.
6. **Persisted series dropped clone data** — `SeriesPoint` gained `clone_*` fields, `emitBucket` copies them, and history.js reads them for clone-strategy docs. Verified: the history timeline replay of the clone run renders real curves (screenshot above) where it used to flatline.
7. **Session clones invisible in race metrics** — lanes now track `good`/`errs` across all ops; for session strategy, clone successes and failures count in reliability while throughput/latency keep tracking pushes, and the science caption says so.
8. **Zero-vs-absent conflation** — the root-cause fix: `WorkloadSpec`'s numeric fields are now pointers. Absent → CLI default (including warmup 10s, killing the dead `-1` sentinel); explicit zeros keep their documented meaning or reach `Validate` and error like the CLI. Covered by new regression tests in `runmgr_test.go`.
9. **run_done dropped at the event cap** — the cap now exempts the terminal event, so day-long soak runs still tell clients they finished.
10. **O(n²) replay redraws** — `timeChart.push()` coalesces through one `requestAnimationFrame`, and race.js batches lane updates (and the pop's forced reflow) the same way; a replay costs one redraw per frame instead of per bucket.

**The 9 secondary findings:** CLI `writeResults` now builds a `results.Doc` and saves through the new `results.Save` (schema lives in one place); `secret_source` resolution runs concurrently across targets (still a synchronous 400 on bad logins); `suggestEntire`'s two CLI calls run in parallel and an unparsed handle is now a discovery error instead of `et/forgemark-/…`; `bench.Target.Secret` carries `json:"-"` so no marshal path can ever leak it; compare-local.sh gets its Entire endpoints from `/api/local/suggest` **and** posts `secret_source` instead of fetching tokens itself — no token touches the script at all anymore; the countdown math and results-saved banner moved to a shared `views/shared.js`; `sample`/`Sample` are one type; the unread `Ops`/`Clones` wire fields are gone; login.sh calls `entire auth status` once.

End-to-end proof: a real GitHub-vs-Entire run through the rewritten script completed clean (both credentials resolved server-side, zero errors), and the README now describes the `secret_source` flow. The server on :8377 is running the fixed build.

Done. The form is restructured and the whole UI now speaks entire.io's design language, verified live across all modes (screenshots above).

**UX — the form now has one obvious starting point.** Instead of dumping every knob at once, it opens on a three-card chooser:
- **Demo race** — prefills the synthetic pair, applies the race preset, opens the race view. No forge, no tokens, and since nothing real is touched, the authorization checkbox is skipped entirely — one click to Start.
- **Compare my forges** — auto-discovers your GitHub + Entire targets from `/api/local/suggest` (the CLI-login path), race-preset applied.
- **Custom run** — the full manual builder.

Everything advanced is now behind progressive disclosure: **workload tuning** collapses into a single row with a live mono summary (`branch · sweep 16 · 60s/level`), and each target's **username / object-format / TLS / entiredb** fields fold into a per-card "Advanced" disclosure that demo targets don't even show. The authorization checkbox only appears when a real (non-demo) target is present, and Start stays gated on it. A "change" link returns to the chooser.

**Design language — matched to entire.io.** I pulled their actual stylesheet and extracted the system: warm near-black surfaces (`#0a0a0a` page, `#151515` cards), the **orange `#fe6e00`** accent (replacing the old blue chrome), warm stone-gray muted text, thin translucent borders, and mono small-caps eyebrow labels like their "ENTIRE CLI" / "SESSIONS" markers. Primary buttons are black-on-orange; checkboxes and focus rings are orange too. Their headline/mono fonts are proprietary woff2, so I used the system mono stack rather than ship files that can't be open-sourced. The categorical chart palette stayed untouched — those are data colors and need to stay distinct from the brand accent.

All JS syntax-checks, `go vet` and the full test suite pass, and the retheme is CSS-variable-driven so it propagated cleanly to the dashboard, race, history, and runs views without per-view edits.

Two notes for the actual open-sourcing, which this didn't touch: you'll want a `LICENSE` file (the README already says MIT) and probably a short `CONTRIBUTING.md` / brief screenshot in the README. Want me to take a pass at repo hygiene — license, contributing guide, a GitHub Actions CI that runs `go test` + the JS syntax checks — as a follow-up?

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# login.sh — authenticate the two CLIs that scripts/compare-local.sh depends
# on: gh (GitHub) and entire (EntireDB). Idempotent: already-valid logins are
# left alone, missing ones launch the CLI's own interactive login flow.
set -euo pipefail

command -v gh >/dev/null || { echo "login: gh CLI not found — install it from https://cli.github.com" >&2; exit 1; }
command -v entire >/dev/null || { echo "login: entire CLI not found — install it from https://docs.entire.io" >&2; exit 1; }

if gh auth status >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "login: gh — already authenticated as $(gh api user --jq .login)"
else
  echo "login: gh — not authenticated, starting gh auth login"
  gh auth login
fi

if ENTIRE_STATUS="$(entire auth status 2>/dev/null)"; then
  echo "login: entire — already authenticated ($(awk '/User:/{print $2}' <<<"$ENTIRE_STATUS") on $(awk '/Context:/{print $2}' <<<"$ENTIRE_STATUS"))"
else
  echo "login: entire — not authenticated, starting entire login"
  entire login
fi

echo "login: both CLIs ready — run scripts/compare-local.sh"

## github.com

github.com is just a generic remote — point `-remote` at it with a PAT
(needs **contents: write**):

```bash
gh repo create you/forgemark-throwaway --private
gh auth token | forgemark -remote https://github.com -token-file - \
  -repos you/forgemark-throwaway -concurrency 1,4 -duration 30s
```

**Keep concurrency low.** github.com applies secondary rate limits and abuse
detection to high-volume content writes; a tight push loop at high concurrency
will get throttled or blocked, and high-volume automated load testing of
github.com isn't sanctioned by their acceptable-use policy. ForgeMark detects a
`github.com` remote and warns above concurrency 16. For a higher-volume
comparison, point `-remote` at a **GitHub Enterprise Server** you control.

## GitLab

GitLab is also a generic remote. The push path wants a **repository-scoped**
credential, which is not always what `glab auth token` returns — so pull the
credential from glab's git-credential helper (username `oauth2`, password a
repo-scoped token):

```bash
glab repo create forgemark-target --private
CRED=$(printf 'protocol=https\nhost=gitlab.com\n\n' | glab auth git-credential get)
printf '%s' "$CRED" | sed -n 's/^password=//p' \
  | forgemark -remote https://gitlab.com -token-file - -user oauth2 \
      -repos you/forgemark-target.git -concurrency 1,8 -duration 1m
```

The web GUI does this for you: pick **glab CLI login** as the credential source
(or **Add from CLI logins**) and the server runs the helper at run start. As
with github.com, gitlab.com rate-limits high-volume writes — keep concurrency
modest, or point `-remote` at a self-managed GitLab you control.

content.text:
GitLab is now a first-class target. "Compare my forges" discovers all three CLIs — **github** (gh CLI login), **gitlab** (glab CLI login), **entire-in** (entire CLI login) — each prefilled with its remote, repo, and credential source, plus a provisioning note.

What I added and verified end to end (real push to gitlab.com, 30 pushes, zero errors, 4 `bench/` branches confirmed on the project):

- **`secret_source: "glab"`** — but GitLab needed more than a token print. `glab auth token` returns an API token that lacks repository scope (I confirmed it 401s on `git ls-remote` with both usernames). GitLab's git auth actually goes through glab's **credential helper**, which returns `username=oauth2` plus a repo-scoped password. So I generalized the secret-source mechanism into two shapes: plain token-printers (gh, entire) and git-credential helpers (glab, fed the target host on stdin). The helper also supplies the username, which the server applies when you haven't set one — so `oauth2` lands automatically. Self-managed GitLab works too, since the helper is queried for the target's actual host.
- **Discovery** — `suggestGitLab()` runs `glab api user`, builds a `<namespace>/forgemark-target.git` target; wired into `/api/local/suggest` alongside github/entire (probed concurrently).
- **Frontend** — credential dropdown gains "glab CLI login"; "Add from CLI logins" and "Compare my forges" now include GitLab.
- **Scripts** — `login.sh` authenticates glab best-effort (optional, skipped with a note if the CLI isn't installed).
- **README** — a GitLab section documenting the credential-helper detail and the `-user oauth2` CLI form, plus a `glab repo create` setup line.
- **Tests** — `parseGitCredential` (the sibling-key trap: `password_expiry_utc` must not be read as the password) and `credHost`.

Full suite passes, JS clean, gofmt clean. One caveat worth stating: like github.com, gitlab.com rate-limits high-volume writes, so the same "keep concurrency modest / point at a self-managed instance for real load" guidance applies — that's in the README.

content.text:
Everything's currently uncommitted on `main` (no branch, no commits yet), so below is the PR draft ready to use once it's on a branch. It's genuinely one large feature PR (~4,700 new lines: 2,628 Go, 1,378 JS, plus CSS/scripts, 6 new test files) since the whole GUI grew in one arc. I've written it in your voice, no em dashes.

---

**Title:**
`Add forgemark serve: a local web GUI with live push-race views, multi-forge comparison, and GitLab support`

**Branch:** `feat/web-gui-race` (suggested; nothing is committed yet)

---

## Body

```markdown
## What this does

Adds `forgemark serve`: a loopback web GUI over the same benchmark engine the
CLI drives, so you can configure a run in the browser, watch several forges
race live, and compare them fairly (every concurrency level starts at the same
instant on all targets). The headline is a **push race** view built for demos,
plus the full charts dashboard for analysis.

It also refactors the engine out of `cmd/forgemark` into `internal/bench` so
the CLI and the server are both thin frontends over one core, adds GitLab as a
first-class target, and reskins the UI to match entire.io.

## What's new

**Web GUI (`internal/server`, `forgemark serve`)**
- Multi-target comparison runs (up to 8), level-aligned, one active run at a
  time so load generators can't perturb each other's numbers.
- Live per-second stats streamed over SSE; a fresh load, a late join, and a
  reconnect are the same code path (replay from Last-Event-ID).
- Embedded single-page UI (no build step, vanilla ES modules): New run,
  Dashboard, Race, Runs, History.
- Binds loopback by default; mutating endpoints reject cross-origin requests.

**Race view (`#race/<id>`)**
- Three metrics you can switch live or deep-link: throughput (cumulative
  successful ops), latency (rolling p50, lower wins, bar length is relative
  speed), and reliability (successful ops / attempts).
- A methodology caption generated from the run's actual workload states exactly
  what is being measured, including that client-side round-trip is in every
  number. Exact ties are called a dead heat, never a false winner.

**Credentials from your CLIs, never pasted**
- A target can carry a `secret_source` (`gh` | `glab` | `entire`) and the
  server pulls the credential from your already-authenticated CLI at run start.
  The token never appears in a request body, a response, or the browser.
- `GET /api/local/suggest` discovers ready-to-run GitHub / GitLab / Entire
  targets from whichever CLIs you're logged into.

**GitLab support**
- Full parity with GitHub in the convenience layer. GitLab's git push needs a
  repository-scoped credential, which `glab auth token` does not always return,
  so the server uses glab's git-credential helper (username `oauth2` plus a
  repo-scoped password), queried for the target's host so self-managed GitLab
  works too.

**Scripts (`scripts/`)**
- `login.sh` authenticates the forge CLIs (glab optional).
- `compare-local.sh` starts a GitHub vs Entire comparison with zero token
  handling and auto-provisions the throwaway repos / mirror / native repo.
- `pushrace.sh` presets the 60s race workload and opens the race view.

**Design**
- Reskinned to entire.io's language: warm near-black surfaces, orange accent,
  mono eyebrow labels.
- New-run form reworked around a start-mode chooser (Compare my forges /
  Custom) with progressive disclosure: workload tuning and per-target advanced
  fields collapse behind disclosures, and an all-demo run skips the
  authorization checkbox since no real host is touched.

**Engine refactor**
- Benchmark engine moved from `cmd/forgemark/*` to `internal/bench`.
- New `internal/results` package owns the result-doc schema and read/write, so
  the CLI (legacy format 1) and server (format 2) share one parser.

## Architecture

One engine, two frontends. `bench.Runner.RunLevel` drives N agents pushing
real git over smart-HTTP through go-git. The CLI sweeps it and prints a table;
the server wraps it for multi-target comparison and streams an event log as
SSE. The frontend derives all state from that stream. Demo (`demo://`) targets
are a synthetic runner so the whole pipeline works offline.

## Safety

This is a load generator that can pull live tokens, so: loopback-only bind with
a warning when `-addr` is not loopback, cross-origin POSTs rejected, the
authorization confirmation preserved for any real target, and `Secret` carries
`json:"-"` so no marshal path can leak it.

## Testing

- `go test ./...` green across bench, results, server, and cmd.
- Verified end to end against real forges: GitHub and GitLab push races (branch
  strategy) and a clone-strategy demo run replayed correctly from History.
- Frontend driven headless across the chooser, both modes, and all three race
  metrics.

## Screenshots

- New-run chooser and Custom mode
- Push race (throughput / latency / reliability)
- Dashboard and History timeline replay

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
```

---

Two things worth flagging before you use it:

**This is big for one PR.** If reviewers would rather digest it in pieces, the natural split is: (1) engine refactor into `internal/bench` + `internal/results`, (2) `forgemark serve` GUI + dashboard, (3) race views, (4) GitLab + CLI-credential sourcing, (5) redesign. Each builds on the last. Happy to carve it up if you want.

**The screenshots section is a placeholder** — GitHub needs them drag-dropped into the textarea. I have real ones in the scratchpad (chooser, race metrics, history replay) if you want me to point you at the files.

Want me to create the branch, commit this in logical chunks, and open the PR with `gh`? I'll only do that on your go-ahead since it pushes and opens outward-facing.

message.content: Maybe we should never have built a web UI, maybe it should have always been the same concepts, but via TUI, which is closer to forgemark originally right?

content.text:
Partly right, but "never" is too strong. The useful way to cut it: forgemark has two jobs, and they point at different interfaces.

**As an operator's instrument, your instinct is correct, and the strongest reason is one we spent a whole review pass papering over.** forgemark is meant to run close to the target, which in practice means a benchmarking box in the same region, reached over SSH. On that box a TUI is native: `ssh in, run forgemark, watch`. The web UI instead means port-forwarding a loopback socket, and worse, it's an HTTP server sitting on a machine holding live forge tokens. Every bit of the `secret_source` indirection, the loopback-origin CSRF guard, the `json:"-"` on the secret, the "is this bound to a real interface" warning, all of that exists to contain a threat model a local TUI process simply doesn't have. It can read `gh auth token` or the env directly and never expose a port. For an open-source load generator, "no network surface, single Go binary, no JS/CSS/SSE to audit" is a real simplicity and safety win, and it keeps the whole project in one language for contributors.

**As a demo artifact, the web UI earns its place.** The race is a presentation you put on a screen for an audience, sometimes a non-technical one. Big animated counters, a podium, latency percentile curves with a legend: pixels beat a terminal there. You are Field CTO; "watch Entire outrun GitHub 20x, live" is a sales moment, and the browser tells that story more legibly than sparklines.

**The good news: almost nothing is wasted.** The refactor put the real work in `internal/bench`, and both the CLI and `serve` are thin frontends over it. A TUI is just a third frontend over the same engine. The only web-specific sunk cost is the server package and the static assets.

What I'd actually do: don't rip out the web UI right before launch, that's churn for no gain. Ship it, but frame `serve`/race explicitly as the demo surface, and add a `forgemark tui` (Bubble Tea over the existing engine) as the primary interactive path for real runs. That gives you the SSH-native, credential-safe daily driver and keeps the shareable demo.

Want me to prototype the TUI over the current engine so you can compare them side by side before deciding what leads?

  ├── internal/server      the web demo, reached only by cmd/forgemark/serve.go
  └── internal/results     shared doc I/O (the engine doesn't even import it)
```

- The engine's `net/http` and `encoding/json` are git transport and the entiredb OAuth exchange. Those were in pre-web forgemark. No HTTP server, no `embed`, no JSON wire shapes for a browser leaked in.
- Exactly one file (`serve.go`) touches the server package. The web is a single amputatable limb.
- The CLI flag surface is the original set (`remote`, `token-file`, `repos`, `strategy`, `concurrency`, ...) plus the entiredb flags that predate the web work. Nothing web-specific bent the CLI.

**The seam that makes "same core, many frontends" work is already there:** `bench.Sink`. The web collector implements it to get live samples; a TUI implements the same interface for its live view. Building the TUI needs zero engine changes. That is the whole payoff of the refactor.

**Nothing needs reverting to be "pure to original."** The only two engine-side changes the web era introduced are the exported `Sink`/`Sample` (frontend-agnostic, the TUI wants it too) and the CLI writing through `internal/results` instead of hand-rolled JSON (behavior-identical, still format-1). Both are improvements, not web contamination.

So the one real decision is how loud the "demo only" boundary should be:

- **Keep `serve` as a subcommand** of the one binary (current). Core stays pure, web runs only if you type `forgemark serve`. Recommended: it is discoverable, and `net/http` is already a transitive dep via go-git, so splitting would not even shrink the core's surface.
- **Split the web into its own binary** (`cmd/forgemark-demo`). A louder quarantine, at the cost of a second install target. Only worth it if you want the statement.

I would keep it as a subcommand and move on. Want me to prototype `forgemark tui` (Bubble Tea over the existing engine and its `Sink`) now, so you can drive a real run in the terminal and compare it head to head with the web race before you lock the direction?

1	# ForgeMark
2	
3	**A concurrent git push/clone throughput benchmark for any smart-HTTP git forge.**
4	
5	ForgeMark measures **sustained push or clone throughput and per-operation
6	latency** the way an agent fleet hits a forge: many concurrent writers, readers,
7	or mixed sessions. It drives **real git operations** through
8	[`go-git`](https://github.com/go-git/go-git) (packfile build + ref update for
9	pushes, upload-pack for clones), so it exercises the forge paths directly — not
10	a synthetic HTTP approximation.
11	
12	It works against **any smart-HTTP git host** — GitLab, Gitea, Bitbucket,
13	self-hosted, GitHub Enterprise Server, github.com, and
14	[Entire](https://github.com/entireio). There's no target flag: the forge is
15	inferred from `-remote` (and, for Entire, from the auth flags you supply).
16	
17	> **Only run ForgeMark against infrastructure you own or are explicitly
18	> authorized to load-test.** A tight push loop is abusive traffic to a host that
19	> hasn't agreed to it.
20	
21	## Install
22	
23	```bash
24	go install github.com/entireio/forgemark/cmd/forgemark@latest
25	```
26	
27	## What it measures
28	
29	Per concurrency level it reports successful operations/sec,
30	p50/p95/p99/p99.9/max latency, and CAS-failure / error counts where they apply.
31	Results print as a table and are written to `results/forgemark-<id>.json` for
32	charting.
33	
34	### Strategies
35	
36	| `-strategy` | shape | what it tells you |
37	|---|---|---|
38	| `branch` (default) | N agents, **one repo**, each pushes its own branch | **Headline single-repo number.** No client-side contention (each agent owns its ref), so it isolates the server's per-repo ref-update path. |
39	| `repo` | N agents spread across **M repos** (`-repo-count`), own branches | Horizontal-scale ceiling — distinct repos serialize independently, so this should scale where `branch` saturates. |
40	| `clone` | N agents, **one repo**, each loops: **shallow-clone** the base branch → discard → repeat | Read-side ceiling: how many concurrent shallow clones/sec the forge sustains, without write load. |
41	| `session` | N agents, each loops: **shallow-clone** the base branch → commit+push `-session-commits` checkpoints to a fresh ephemeral branch → abandon → repeat | Realistic agent lifecycle: interleaves **read load (clone) with write load (push)** on one repo. Reports clone and push latencies separately. |
42	
43	## Usage
44	
45	Two steps: **set up the target repos**, then **run**.
46	
47	### 1. Set up targets
48	
49	ForgeMark does not create repos — it pushes to ones you provide. Create them on
50	your forge and make sure your credential can push:
51	
52	- **`branch`** needs **one empty repo**.
53	- **`repo`** needs **M empty repos**.
54	- **`clone`** and **`session`** need a repo with a **base branch that has
55	  content** to clone. An empty repo degrades to a no-read orphan, so a read-side
56	  run against an unseeded repo isn't measuring what you think — push a base
57	  branch first.
58	
59	Per forge, roughly:
60	
61	```bash
62	# GitHub (needs the gh CLI): a throwaway private repo
63	gh repo create you/forgemark-target --private
64	# for clone/session runs, give it content:
65	#   git clone … && git commit --allow-empty -m base && git push
66	
67	# GitLab / Gitea / self-hosted: create an empty repo in the UI or via the
68	# forge's API, ensure your token/user can push, and (for clone/session) push a
69	# base branch with at least one commit.
70	```
71	
72	### 2. Run
73	
74	Most forges just need a token. Point `-remote` at the host and supply the token
75	via `-token-file` (a file, or `-` for stdin):
76	
77	```bash
78	FORGE="-remote https://git.example.com"
79	
80	# Headline: single-repo throughput, sweep concurrency
81	# (-token-file reads a file; use "-" to pipe the token in on stdin instead)
82	forgemark $FORGE -token-file ~/.forge-token \
83	  -repos org/repo -concurrency 1,8,32 -duration 2m
84	
85	# Spread across 16 repos (horizontal scale)
86	forgemark $FORGE -token-file ~/.forge-token -strategy repo \
87	  -repo-pattern "org/bench-{n}" -repo-count 16 -concurrency 32,128 -duration 2m
88	
89	# Clone: read-side throughput, discard each in-memory clone (needs a seeded base branch)
90	forgemark $FORGE -token-file ~/.forge-token -repos org/repo \
91	  -strategy clone -clone-depth 1 -concurrency 8,32 -duration 2m
92	
93	# Session: clone + push 5 checkpoints, abandon, repeat (needs a seeded base branch)
94	forgemark $FORGE -token-file ~/.forge-token -repos org/repo \
95	  -strategy session -session-commits 5 -clone-depth 1 -concurrency 8,32
96	```
97	
98	The push URL is `<-remote>/<repo>` — the `-repos` value is appended **verbatim**
99	(ForgeMark does no path rewriting), so include a `.git` suffix if your forge
100	needs it. The token is used as the basic-auth password with a conventional
101	username (`-user` to override); most forges accept a PAT this way. The secret
102	comes from `-token-file` or the `ACCESS_TOKEN` env var — never a CLI flag, so it
103	can't leak via `ps` or shell history. Entire needs a couple of extra flags — see
104	below.
105	
106	## Entire
107	
108	Entire needs two extra flags — `-token-url` and `-jurisdiction`. Auth is a
109	single short-lived **jurisdiction identity token**: ForgeMark exchanges your
110	subject token for it (RFC 8693) and refreshes it, so one token authorizes every
111	repo you can reach. Pass the subject token as `-token-file`/`ACCESS_TOKEN`:
112	
113	```bash
114	forgemark -remote https://aws-us-east-2.entire.io \
115	  -token-url    https://us.auth.entire.io/oauth/token \
116	  -jurisdiction https://us.entire.io \
117	  -token-file   ~/.entire-subject-token \
118	  -repos your/repo -concurrency 1,8,32,128 -duration 2m
119	```
120	
121	`-repos` is appended verbatim — ForgeMark does no path rewriting, so pass the
122	full repo path exactly as your Entire deployment expects it. The exact form is
123	deployment-specific — see the runbook.
124	
125	Deployment-specific setup (obtaining the subject token, target provisioning) and
126	methodology notes live in Entire's own runbook.
127	
128	## github.com
129	
130	github.com is just a generic remote — point `-remote` at it with a PAT
131	(needs **contents: write**):
132	
133	```bash
134	gh repo create you/forgemark-throwaway --private
135	gh auth token | forgemark -remote https://github.com -token-file - \
136	  -repos you/forgemark-throwaway -concurrency 1,4 -duration 30s
137	```
138	
139	**Keep concurrency low.** github.com applies secondary rate limits and abuse
140	detection to high-volume content writes; a tight push loop at high concurrency
141	will get throttled or blocked, and high-volume automated load testing of
142	github.com isn't sanctioned by their acceptable-use policy. ForgeMark detects a
143	`github.com` remote and warns above concurrency 16. For a higher-volume
144	comparison, point `-remote` at a **GitHub Enterprise Server** you control.
145	
146	## Key flags
147	
148	| flag | default | notes |
149	|---|---|---|
150	| `-remote` | — | base URL of the forge (e.g. `https://gitlab.com`); the cluster base URL for Entire |
151	| `-token-file` | — | file holding the credential secret; `-` reads stdin (else `$ACCESS_TOKEN`) |
152	| `-user` | `x-access-token` | basic-auth username (token forges ignore it) |
153	| `-repos` / `-repo-pattern`+`-repo-count` | — | target repo path(s), appended verbatim; `-repo-pattern` expands `{n}` to `1..N` |
154	| `-strategy` | `branch` | `branch` \| `repo` \| `clone` \| `session` |
155	| `-branch-prefix` | — | prepended verbatim to branch names, before the run ID (e.g. `bench/` → `refs/heads/bench/fm...`); groups branches for easy cleanup |
156	| `-concurrency` | `1,8,32,128` | swept sequentially, one row each |
157	| `-duration` / `-warmup` | `60s` / `10s` | measured window / discarded ramp |
158	| `-files-min`/`-files-max`/`-file-size` | `1`/`10`/`2048` | commit shape; ignored by `clone` |
159	| `-object-format` | `auto` | `sha1` \| `sha256`; `auto` probes the Entire advertisement (generic/github default sha1) |
160	| `-session-commits` | `5` | session strategy checkpoints per cloned session |

Here's the draft for the core PR. Focused on the "reusable engine, no behavior change" story, since it's the base of the stack.

---

**Title:** `refactor: extract a reusable benchmark engine (internal/bench + internal/results)`

**Base:** `main`  **Compare:** `refactor/engine-core`

---

## Body

```markdown
## What this does

Splits forgemark into a reusable core and a thin CLI, so future interactive
frontends can drive the same engine without the CLI knowing anything about
them. This is a pure structural refactor: the CLI's flags, output, and behavior
are unchanged.

It's the first of a short stack. The web demo and a TUI both build on this core
as follow-up PRs; nothing web-specific lands here.

## Why

The engine lived in `package main` alongside the flag parsing, so anything that
wanted to drive a run had to be the CLI. Lifting the engine into its own package
lets several frontends share one core and keeps that core honest: no UI concern
can leak into the benchmark path.

## Changes

- **`internal/bench`** is the concurrent push/clone engine (agents, creds,
  endpoint, session, stats) plus `Runner` / `Workload` / `Target` config, moved
  out of `cmd/forgemark`. It exposes a frontend-agnostic `Sink` so any UI can
  observe samples live as they're recorded. The CLI passes `nil` and summarizes
  post-hoc exactly as before. The package has no dependency on any frontend, the
  result-doc format, or an HTTP server.
- **`internal/results`** is one owner of the run-document schema and its
  read/write. The CLI's legacy single-target docs and the multi-target shape a
  UI would produce share a single parser (`Load` normalizes the legacy form),
  so history tooling only ever sees one shape.
- **`cmd/forgemark`** keeps the same CLI surface and behavior, now a thin flag
  layer over the engine that persists results through `internal/results`
  instead of hand-building JSON.

## Not in this PR

No web server, no `serve` subcommand, no TUI, no scripts. Those are the
follow-up branches that sit on top of this one.

## Testing

- `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, and `go test ./...` all green
  (bench, results, cmd).
- The engine files move as git renames, so `git blame` history is preserved.
- CLI smoke-checked: same flags, same table output, same
  `results/forgemark-<id>.json`.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
```

---

One note before you use it: the "no user-visible CLI change" claim is the load-bearing one for reviewers, and it's true for flags and output, but I did make one small internal swap that's worth being able to defend if asked. The CLI now writes its results doc through `internal/results` rather than the old hand-rolled `map[string]any`. The on-disk format is byte-compatible with what the CLI wrote before (same field names, same legacy shape), so existing tooling and history still parse it. If you'd rather the PR claim zero behavior change with no asterisks, I can point you at the exact `writeResults` diff so you can eyeball the output equivalence, or I can add a golden-file test that pins the CLI's JSON output.

Want me to push the branch and open the PR with this, or adjust the draft first?

content.text:
Reviewed PR #11 against its diff (local checkout is exactly at the PR head). It's a clean extraction; the substantive review is on the four genuinely-new/changed files, not the renames.

## Overview

Lifts the engine out of `package main` into `internal/bench` (with a frontend-agnostic `Sink`) and `internal/results`, leaving `cmd/forgemark` a thin flag layer. Behavior-preserving by design. Builds, vets, and tests pass.

## What's solid

- **The `Sink` seam is the right abstraction.** `NewRunner(..., sink)` with the CLI passing `nil` keeps the engine frontend-agnostic without special-casing. This is the whole point of the refactor and it lands cleanly.
- **`internal/bench` has no outward dependencies** — no results package, no server, no HTTP server. The one purity boundary that matters is intact.
- **`NewRunner` orders its guards safely**: `w.Validate()` runs before `slices.Max(w.Concurrency)`, and Validate rejects empty concurrency, so the max can't panic.
- **Security is preserved**: `Target.Secret` carries `json:"-"`, `readSecret` keeps the token off argv, no secret is logged.
- **`results` test coverage is good**: round-trip, legacy normalization, path-traversal rejection, List skip/sort/missing-dir.

## Findings (all low severity)

- **The "byte-compatible" result output claim is slightly wrong** (`writeResults`, main.go:253). The old CLI marshaled a `map[string]any`, which Go emits with **alphabetically sorted keys**; the new code marshals a `results.Doc` struct, emitted in **field-declaration order**. Same fields, same values, parses identically through `Load`, but the serialized key order changed, so it is *semantically* compatible, not byte-identical. Also `Levels` has `json:"levels,omitempty"`, so a run cancelled before any level completes now omits the key where the old code wrote `"levels":null`. Neither breaks any parser, but the PR body should say "format-compatible" rather than imply identical bytes.
- **`results.Save` is not directly tested** — it's the CLI's actual write path (arbitrary `-out`, parent-dir mkdir), only exercised transitively via `Write` with a validated filename. A one-line test writing to a nested `-out dir/sub/x.json` would pin the branch the CLI depends on. If you want the compatibility claim ironclad, a golden-file test on the CLI's JSON output covers both this and the point above.
- **Minor error-precedence change**: `readSecret` now runs in `run()` before `NewRunner`, so if both `-remote` and the credential are missing, the user now sees the credential error first instead of `-remote required`. Cosmetic.

## Verdict

Ship it. No correctness or security issues; the findings are cosmetic or test-coverage nits. The only thing I'd actually change before merge is softening "byte-compatible" in the PR description (or adding the golden test to make it true). Everything else can be a follow-up.

## What this does

Splits forgemark into a reusable core and a thin CLI, so future interactive
frontends can drive the same engine without the CLI knowing anything about
them. This is a pure structural refactor: the CLI's flags, output, and behavior
are unchanged.

## Why

The engine lived in `package main` alongside the flag parsing, so anything that
wanted to drive a run had to be the CLI. Lifting the engine into its own package
lets several frontends share one core and keeps that core honest: no UI concern
can leak into the benchmark path.

## Changes

- **`internal/bench`** is the concurrent push/clone engine (agents, creds,
  endpoint, session, stats) plus `Runner` / `Workload` / `Target` config, moved
  out of `cmd/forgemark`. It exposes a frontend-agnostic `Sink` so any UI can
  observe samples live as they're recorded. The CLI passes `nil` and summarizes
  post-hoc exactly as before. The package has no dependency on any frontend, the
  result-doc format, or an HTTP server.
- **`internal/results`** is one owner of the run-document schema and its
  read/write. The CLI's legacy single-target docs and the multi-target shape a
  UI would produce share a single parser (`Load` normalizes the legacy form),
  so history tooling only ever sees one shape.
- **`cmd/forgemark`** keeps the same CLI surface and behavior, now a thin flag
  layer over the engine that persists results through `internal/results`
  instead of hand-building JSON.

## Testing

- `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, and `go test ./...` all green
  (bench, results, cmd).
- The engine files move as git renames, so `git blame` history is preserved.
- CLI smoke-checked: same flags, same table output, same
  `results/forgemark-<id>.json`.

content.text:
`high effort → 3+5 angles × 6 candidates → 1-vote verify (recall-biased) → ≤10 findings`

You are reviewing for **recall** at high effort: catch every real bug a careful
reviewer would catch in one sitting. At this level, catching real bugs matters
more than avoiding false positives. Err on the side of surfacing.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Find candidates (3 correctness angles + 3 cleanup angles + 1 altitude angle + 1 conventions angle, up to 6 each)

Run **8 independent finder angles** via the Agent tool. Each
surfaces **up to 6 candidate findings** with `file`, `line`, a one-line
`summary`, and a concrete `failure_scenario`.

### Angle A — line-by-line diff scan

Read every hunk in the diff, line by line. Then Read the enclosing function for
each hunk — bugs in unchanged lines of a touched function are in scope (the PR
re-exposes or fails to fix them). For every line ask: what input, state, timing,
or platform makes this line wrong? Look for inverted/wrong conditions,
off-by-one, null/undefined deref, missing `await`, falsy-zero checks,
wrong-variable copy-paste, error swallowed in catch, unescaped regex metachars.

### Angle B — removed-behavior auditor

For every line the diff DELETES or replaces, name the invariant or behavior it
enforced, then search the new code for where that invariant is re-established.
If you can't find it, that's a candidate: a removed guard, a dropped error
path, a narrowed validation, a deleted test that was covering a real case.

### Angle C — cross-file tracer

For each function the diff changes, find its callers (Grep for the symbol) and
check whether the change breaks any call site: a new precondition, a changed
return shape, a new exception, a timing/ordering dependency. Also check callees:
does a parallel change in the same PR make a call unsafe?

### Reuse

The angles above hunt for bugs; this one and the next two hunt for cleanup in
the changed code. Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

### Conventions (CLAUDE.md)

Find the CLAUDE.md files that govern the changed code: the user-level
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, the repo-root CLAUDE.md, plus any CLAUDE.md or
CLAUDE.local.md in a directory that is an ancestor of a changed file (a
directory's CLAUDE.md only applies to files at or below it). Read each one
that exists, then check the diff for clear violations of the rules they state.

Only flag a violation when you can quote the exact rule and the exact line
that breaks it — no style preferences, no vague "spirit of the doc"
inferences. In the finding, name the CLAUDE.md path and quote the rule so the
report can cite it. If no CLAUDE.md applies, return nothing for this angle.

Cleanup, altitude, and conventions candidates use the same
`file`/`line`/`summary` shape; in `failure_scenario`, state the concrete
cost (what is duplicated, wasted, harder to maintain, or which CLAUDE.md rule
is broken) instead of a crash. Correctness bugs always outrank cleanup,
altitude, and conventions findings when the output cap forces a cut.

Pass every candidate with a nameable failure scenario through — finders that
silently drop half-believed candidates bypass the verify step and are the
dominant cause of misses.

## Phase 2 — Verify (1-vote, recall-biased)

Dedup near-duplicates (same defect, same location, same reason → keep one). For
each remaining candidate, run **one verifier** via the Agent tool:
give it the diff, the relevant file(s), and the candidate; it returns exactly
one of **CONFIRMED / PLAUSIBLE / REFUTED**.

**PLAUSIBLE by default** — do not refute a candidate for being "speculative" or
"depends on runtime state" when the state is realistic: concurrency races,
nil/undefined on a rare-but-reachable path (error handler, cold cache, missing
optional field), falsy-zero treated as missing, off-by-one on a boundary the
code does not exclude, retry storms / partial failures, regex/allowlist that
lost an anchor. These are PLAUSIBLE.

**REFUTED** only when constructible from the code: factually wrong (quote the
actual line); provably impossible (type/constant/invariant — show it); already
handled in this diff (cite the guard); or pure style with no observable effect.

Keep **CONFIRMED and PLAUSIBLE**. Drop REFUTED.

## Output

Return findings as a JSON array of at most 10 objects:

```json
[
  {
    "file": "path/to/file.ext",
    "line": 123,
    "summary": "one-sentence statement of the bug",
    "failure_scenario": "concrete inputs/state → wrong output/crash"
  }
]
```

Ranked most-severe first. If more than 10 survive, keep the 10 most
severe. If nothing survives verification, return `[]`.

1	// forgemark — a concurrent git-push load generator for any smart-HTTP git forge.
2	//
3	// It answers the headline question: how many small pushes/sec can one repo
4	// sustain under many concurrent writers, and what's the per-push latency
5	// distribution? It drives REAL pushes through go-git (packfile build + ref
6	// update), so unlike a plain HTTP load tool it exercises the full receive-pack
7	// path.
8	//
9	// The forge is inferred from the flags, not an explicit -target:
10	//
11	//	any smart-HTTP host (GitLab, Gitea, Bitbucket, self-hosted, GHES, github.com)
12	//	    — push to <-remote>/<repo> (repo path appended verbatim; include a .git
13	//	    suffix in -repos if the forge needs it) with a static credential from the
14	//	    environment. A github.com remote additionally gets the abuse-detection
15	//	    warning above concurrency 16.
16	//	entiredb — selected by supplying -token-url and -jurisdiction: one
17	//	    jurisdiction identity token (RFC 8693 exchange, authorized live per push),
18	//	    direct-to-node push, node discovery via X-Entire-Replicas.
19	//
20	// Strategies (-strategy): branch (default; per-agent branches on one repo),
21	// repo (spread across N repos), clone (clone-only read loop), session
22	// (clone+push loop per agent).
23	//
24	// The benchmark engine itself lives in internal/bench; this package is the
25	// flag-driven CLI over it.
26	//
27	// Only ever run this against infrastructure you own or are explicitly
28	// authorized to load-test.
29	package main
30	
31	import (
32		"context"
33		"errors"
34		"flag"
35		"fmt"
36		"io"
37		"os"
38		"os/signal"
39		"slices"
40		"strconv"
41		"strings"
42		"syscall"
43		"time"
44	
45		"github.com/entireio/forgemark/internal/bench"
46		"github.com/entireio/forgemark/internal/results"
47	)
48	
49	func main() {
50		if err := run(); err != nil {
51			fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "forgemark: "+err.Error())
52			os.Exit(1)
53		}
54	}
55	
56	// cliConfig is the parsed flag set: the single benchmark target, the shared
57	// workload shape, and CLI-only concerns (where the secret comes from, where
58	// results go).
59	type cliConfig struct {
60		target    bench.Target
61		workload  bench.Workload
62		tokenFile string // path to the credential secret ("-" = stdin); preferred over $ACCESS_TOKEN
63		out       string
64	}
65	
66	func run() error {
67		cfg, err := parseFlags()
68		if err != nil {
69			return err
70		}
71	
72		secret, err := readSecret(cfg.tokenFile)
73		if err != nil {
74			return err
75		}
76		cfg.target.Secret = secret
77	
78		// github.com throttles high-volume writes; warn on stderr before a sweep
79		// that's likely to trip its abuse detection.
80		if cfg.target.TokenURL == "" && cfg.target.Jurisdiction == "" && bench.IsGitHubDotCom(cfg.target.Remote) {
81			if hi := slices.Max(cfg.workload.Concurrency); hi > 16 {
82				fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "forgemark: warning: concurrency %d against github.com is likely to trip "+

content.text:
I did the homework, and there's an important gap to surface before I propose anything: **"Runners" isn't a public Entire concept.** I checked the CLI (no `runner` verb; the closest are `session`, `dispatch`, `labs`, `agent`), the docs index (`llms.txt`), and the glossary. The public model is all about **sessions, checkpoints, dispatches, and mirrors**. Runners, Trails, and Gates appear only in your internal context, so they're clearly roadmap/internal and you know them far better than any doc will tell me.

So rather than build a plan on a guessed definition, here's my **working model** of an Entire Runner, then a compact idea cut. Correct the model and I'll harden the plan around it.

**My working model of an Entire Runner:** a managed, triggered, repeatable execution unit that runs a defined job close to the repo/data (Entire already mirrors repos regionally "for maximum agent throughput"), emits results Entire records as sessions/checkpoints, and can be fronted by a Gate (a pass/fail check) and sequenced in a Trail (a workflow). Essentially CI runners, but native to Entire's agent-SDLC and regional footprint.

**Why forgemark fits this unusually well:** forgemark's own README says the one thing you must do for valid numbers is *run the generator close to the target, same region*. Today that means manually SSHing to a box in-region. Entire already has regional clusters (us/eu/au/in) and mirrors. A forgemark Runner is the missing piece that makes "benchmark the forge from where the agents actually are" a one-click, repeatable thing.

**The runner taxonomy I'd propose, ranked:**

1. **Regional runner** (the headline). Entire schedules forgemark into a cluster's region and benchmarks that cluster from-region, so numbers aren't RTT-dominated by a laptop. This is the differentiated one and it directly exploits Entire's regional + mirror infrastructure. Heaviest to build (needs the in-region execution + phone-home path).

2. **Scheduled canary runner.** Runs a benchmark suite on a cron, stores each run as an Entire session/checkpoint, tracks throughput/latency as a trend, and flags regressions. Turns forgemark from a one-shot into continuous forge-health monitoring.

3. **CI / Gate runner.** Runs a benchmark as a PR or deploy check and gates on thresholds (p95 ceiling, ops/s floor), exit-code + annotation. This is a "Gate" in your terms, and it's the smallest, most concrete first step. Notably, **open PR #6 already adds threshold flags for CI regression gating** — the gating primitive is being built, so a runner just wraps it.

4. **Matrix runner.** Headless, distributed version of the race: same workload across forges × regions × strategies, aggregated into one comparison. The race view becomes its report.

**How it lands architecturally** (no engine rework): keep `internal/bench` (engine) and `internal/results` (doc format). A "runner" is just another headless driver over the engine plus a **result sink** — local JSON today, plus new sinks for Entire (store via `entire api`) and CI (annotation + threshold exit code). Trail = a named suite of runs; Gate = a threshold check over a run's results.

**My recommendation on sequencing:** CI/Gate first as the MVP (leverages PR #6, smallest, immediately useful), then scheduled canary (adds trend/regression + Entire storage), then the regional runner as the strategic headline once the managed-execution path exists.

Two things I need from you before I write the full plan:

1. **Correct my Runner model** — especially how Runners relate to Trails and Gates, and whether a Runner is Entire-managed compute (my assumption) or a client-side concept.
2. **Which end to start from** — the strategic headline (regional, managed) or the pragmatic MVP (CI/Gate on top of PR #6)?

content.text:
Found the real thing, and it sharpens the plan a lot. Here's what an Entire Runner actually is, then the forgemark plan grounded in it.

## What a Runner is (from `.entire/runners/*.json` in the cli and git-sync repos)

A Runner is a declarative job file: `scope: trail` (a branch's changes vs its base), triggered on `push`/`api`, executed in a sandbox with a scoped repo token, producing a typed `output`. The `entire runner setup/tune` command scaffolds them (hidden "during maturation", which is why it's absent from the public docs). The stock set is seven: `summary`, `review`, `review-focus`, `risk`, `security`, `confidence`, `drift`.

Three output types matter:
- **`trail_summary`** — markdown (the Problem/Solution summary).
- **`code_review_comments`** — inline findings with severity/confidence/location.
- **`trail_monitor`** — a scored metric: `{key, label, value_type: percent, polarity: lower_is_better|higher_is_better}`, value 0-100. This is the gateable signal (Risk, Security, Drift are all monitors).

## The key insight

**All seven stock runners are `prompt_runner`s: an LLM reads a diff and judges it.** None of them *run* anything. forgemark would be the first **execution-based runner that emits measured, empirical signals** into the exact same Trail machinery. A forgemark benchmark maps perfectly onto `trail_monitor`: throughput (higher_is_better), p95 latency (lower_is_better), error/CAS rate (lower_is_better). So instead of an LLM guessing whether a change is risky, forgemark tells the Trail what the change actually did to forge performance, and it shows up next to Risk and Security and can back a Gate.

## The forgemark runner set I'd propose

Concrete `.entire/runners/*.json`, each a benchmark that runs on push and emits a monitor:

| Runner | Output | Metric | Polarity |
|---|---|---|---|
| `trail-throughput` | trail_monitor | push ops/s (branch sweep) | higher_is_better |
| `trail-latency` | trail_monitor | p95 ms | lower_is_better |
| `trail-forge-errors` | trail_monitor | error + CAS rate | lower_is_better |
| `trail-perf` | trail_summary | the race table rendered as markdown | — |

That's the demo race, but headless, per-branch, and gateable.

## The two build layers

**1. Definitions + a forgemark output adapter (small, mostly in this repo).** The runners are JSON, but forgemark needs a machine-readable *monitor* mode: reduce a `results.Doc` to the runner's `{"value": <n>, "rationale": "..."}` last-JSON-line contract. A `forgemark report --emit monitor` (or a `--format entire`) over the existing engine + `internal/results`. Cheap, and it's the seam everything else hangs off.

**2. The runtime (the real work, needs Entire).** Every stock runner uses the read-only `claude` sandbox. forgemark is different: it needs the forgemark binary, **network egress to the target forge**, and ideally **regional placement** (forgemark's whole methodology caveat is "run close to the target"). That's a new runner profile, and it's exactly where Entire's regional clusters + mirrors are the differentiator. Two ways to get the `runtime.kind`:
- Reuse `prompt_runner` as an MVP: a runner whose prompt is "run `forgemark ...`, emit the result JSON as the last line" (works with today's adapter, if the sandbox allows egress).
- A proper non-prompt kind. I saw hints of `agent_runner`, `trail_runner`, and one `script_runner` reference but no `command_runner`/`exec_runner`, so a measured/exec runner kind looks like a genuine gap forgemark would be the first real user of.

## Sequencing

1. **forgemark monitor-output mode** — the adapter (this repo, no Entire dependency).
2. **CI/Gate proof** — wire it into GitHub Actions on top of open PR #6's threshold flags: forgemark runs, emits the monitor value, gates the PR. Proves the signal with zero new Entire infra.
3. **Native Entire runner** — the regional, egress-capable runtime that runs forgemark in-region and posts monitors to the Trail. The strategic headline.

## What I need from you

1. Does a Gate already threshold a `trail_monitor` (so `throughput < X` fails a Trail), or is Gate still to build? That decides whether forgemark just emits and rides existing gating, or we build the gate too.
2. Is there an exec/command/`script_runner` runtime, or would forgemark be the case that justifies one? This is the biggest scope fork.
3. Sandbox reality: can a runner sandbox make outbound git connections and be pinned to a region? That's the gating constraint on the native runner.

Want me to draft the four runner JSON files and the `forgemark report --emit monitor` adapter as a concrete first PR (layer 1), so there's something real to run in CI while the runtime questions get answered?

## What this does

Adds `forgemark serve`: a loopback web GUI over the same engine the CLI drives,
framed as the demo surface (the CLI stays the operator's tool). Configure a run
in the browser, drive real git push/clone load against one or more forges at
once, and watch them race live. Builds on the merged engine refactor (#11); the
CLI and the trail runners on `main` are untouched.

## What's new

**`forgemark serve` (internal/server)**
- Multi-target comparison runs, one active at a time, every concurrency level
  started simultaneously so the overlay is a fair comparison.
- A per-target collector implements `bench.Sink` and rolls 10s-window
  percentiles; an append-only event log fans out over SSE and replays from
  `Last-Event-ID`, so a fresh load, a late join, and a reconnect are one path.
- `demo://` targets are a synthetic runner so the whole pipeline works offline.

**Live race view (`#race/<id>`)**
- A head-to-head with three metrics (throughput, latency, reliability),
  switchable live and deep-linkable, plus a methodology caption generated from
  the run's actual workload. Exact ties are called a dead heat.

**Credentials from your CLIs, never pasted**
- A target names a `secret_source` (`gh` | `glab` | `entire`) and the server
  pulls the credential from your authenticated CLI at run start, so the browser
  never holds a token. `GET /api/local/suggest` prefills GitHub / GitLab /
  Entire targets. GitLab goes through glab's git-credential helper (a
  repository-scoped token even when glab's API token isn't).

**Scripts** — `login.sh`, `compare-local.sh` (zero token handling,
auto-provisions the throwaway repos / mirror / native repo), `pushrace.sh`.

**Design** — the New-run form is a start-mode chooser with progressive
disclosure; the whole UI is styled to entire.io's warm-black + orange language.

## Safety

It's a load generator that can pull live tokens: loopback-only bind with a
warning when `-addr` isn't loopback, cross-origin POSTs rejected, and
`Target.Secret` carries `json:"-"` so no marshal path can leak it.

## Testing

- `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `go test ./...` all green; JS and scripts
  syntax-checked; live smoke of `serve` plus GitHub / GitLab / Entire runs.
- The final commit applies a full `/code-review` pass over this branch
  (latency-gate blanking, an allDemo/blank-target mismatch, secret-exec ordering
  before the active-run check, `serve -h` exit code, a script cluster wiring
  bug, and CSS/dead-state cleanups), each with a test or live check.

I dug into this end-to-end. Here's the diagnosis: **your runner config is correct and in the right place. The problem is that the automatic trail-runner pipeline isn't executing for `entireio/forgemark`, which is a server-side enablement issue, not a repo-file issue.**

Evidence I gathered:

- **Configs are valid and present where the trail engine reads them.** All five `.entire/runners/*.json` parse, are `enabled: true`, `scope: trail`, and include `push` triggers (review/risk/security/summary), and they exist on **both `origin/main` and `origin/feat/web-demo`**. So it's not a missing-file or wrong-ref problem.
- **`entire runner setup` only writes/tailors those files** — it's not a server registration handshake. So merging the files via PR is the whole config story; nothing was skipped there.
- **The repo is mirrored** to Entire (3 clusters), and pushes to `feat/web-demo` happened *after* the runners were live on main. So a push-triggered runner should have fired, and didn't.

That leaves the automatic push → trail-engine → runner-execution pipeline itself. Ranked by likelihood:

1. **The trail-runner engine isn't turned on for this repo.** Mirroring a repo (for benchmarks/sessions) is not the same as onboarding it to the trail evaluator. Working examples like `entireio/git-sync` and `entireio/cli` fire runners because they're wired to the trail engine (webhook/App + trail feature enabled). forgemark looks mirrored-but-not-trail-enabled.
2. **Maturation gate.** `entire runner` is explicitly "hidden during maturation," and there's a pending **CLI 0.8.42 → 0.9.0** bump. If runner execution went live in 0.9.0 and the rollout is version/beta-gated, forgemark may not be enrolled yet.
3. **Trigger delivery** — the push event isn't reaching the trail engine for this repo (a subset of #1).

Immediate workaround to get a review on the trail right now, without the auto-pipeline: `entire review --set-output trail` runs the multi-agent reviewer on the current branch and posts the verdict to the trail.

Two things only you can confirm from the Entire backend, and they'll pin it exactly:
- **How is the trail engine triggered for a repo** — GitHub App/webhook on push, or off a mirror sync — and does `entireio/forgemark` have that wiring? (My bet is no.)
- **Does runner execution require 0.9.0 / beta enrollment**, and is this repo enrolled?

One aside so it doesn't mislead you: when I tried to `git ls-remote` the Entire mirror to check sync, it returned "invalid or expired token" — that's just my local jurisdiction git token being stale (my `entire auth` for the mirror), unrelated to the trail engine, which runs server-side regardless of my token. Want me to `brew upgrade entire` to 0.9.0 and re-push a trivial commit to see if the runners fire on the newer CLI, as a quick test of hypothesis #2?

Traced it to the source. Here's the answer, and it's more specific than "not wired."

**Where the wiring comes from:** the Entire **GitHub App**. `entire enable` posts to `/api/v1/cli/enable`, which records the repo and reports whether the App can reach it (returning an `InstallURL` to the App install page when it can't). Push events delivered through that App drive the trail engine, which reads the per-repo `.entire/runners/*.json` and runs each one over a trail (a branch-vs-base diff). For forgemark this wiring **is present and healthy**: the mirror record shows `status: ready`, `installationId: 104585035`, cell `aws-us-east-2`, and the trail engine already created the trail for your PR.

**So it's not the App and not the runner files. The actual failure is one step downstream:** the trail (`#2`, id `01KYKH3VQNRHF5TDKWR8RM9MDE`) is stuck at `phase: building` with **`baseSha: null` and `mergeBaseSha: null`**. Every runner prompt diffs `origin/{{base_branch}}...HEAD`, so with no resolved base the engine has no diff to hand them. Nothing runs, which is exactly what you see: `monitors: []`, zero review comments, no runner executions. The head SHA (`d89139e`) is correct; only the base against `main` never resolved.

**Why the base is null:** the trail engine couldn't compute the merge-base of your head against `main` on the Entire side. That's a base/mirror resolution problem, not a repo problem. Most likely the mirror's `main` history needed to compute the merge-base isn't fully ingested (your branch was rebased onto the just-merged `d15ceaf`, so the engine needs the mirror to have `main` at `d15ceaf` to find the base). The trail sitting in `building` for hours with a null base is the tell.

**What I'd do to confirm and unstick it:**
- Have the backend look at trail `01KYKH3VQNRHF5TDKWR8RM9MDE` and check why base/merge-base resolution didn't complete (mirror `main` ingest for `entireio/forgemark`, cell `aws-us-east-2`).
- Fast local test of the hypothesis: push one trivial commit to `feat/web-demo`. That re-triggers trail building; if the mirror now has `main`, the base should resolve, the phase should advance past `building`, and the push-triggered runners (review/risk/security/summary) should fire. If `baseSha` stays null after that, it's a mirror-sync bug on the Entire side, not timing.

Want me to push a no-op commit to re-trigger it and re-query the trail to see whether `baseSha` resolves? That will tell us in about a minute whether this is a one-time stuck trail or a persistent sync gap for the repo.

This accepts every loopback Origin regardless of port, so a hostile page served by another local development server can send a simple text/plain JSON POST without preflight and drive runs or CLI-sourced credentials. secret_source is resolved and attached to any caller-supplied remote or token URL without validating its audience. For example, pairing "gh" with an attacker-controlled remote sends the GitHub token as Basic Auth, while an Entire token can be POSTed to an arbitrary token_url; reject source/target mismatches and pin exchange endpoints before materializing credentials.

AI
Trail Review
internal/server/collector.go:93
11h ago

The snapshot holds the collector mutex while concatenating every latency in the ten-second window. At benchmark-scale throughput this blocks all concurrent OnSample calls once per second, delaying agents before their next operation and depressing measured throughput; copy or swap slice headers under lock and concatenate after unlocking.

AI
Trail Review
internal/server/runmgr.go:440
11h ago

Launching one goroutine per target is not a start barrier because RunLevel constructs all agents and starts its timeout internally. Target-dependent setup time therefore shifts measured windows and breaks the promised level-aligned comparison; prepare every runner first, wait for readiness, then release them with one shared start signal.

Trail Review
internal/server/runmgr.go:425
11h ago

The level index is advanced before each collector is reset while the ticker runs independently. A tick during this transition snapshots the previous level's remaining samples and emits/persists them under the new level index; synchronize the transition and flush or discard the old bucket before changing levelIdx.

internal/server/collector.go:58
11h ago

bench.Sink explicitly receives warm-up samples, but this collector records them unconditionally. Live charts, race totals/reliability, and persisted series therefore include warm-up even though the authoritative level result excludes it; filter by Sample.Offset or reset precisely at the warm-up boundary.

fix: address trail-review findings on the web server

Security (High):
- server.go: require the request Origin to match the server's own host:port,
  not just any loopback hostname. A loopback-only check accepted any other
  local dev server (a different port is still cross-origin), letting a hostile
  page drive runs and CLI-sourced credentials via a simple no-preflight POST.
- runmgr.go/local.go: pin each secret_source to its issuer's audience before
  materializing the credential (gh→github.com, glab→gitlab.com, entire→
  *.entire.io for remote/token_url/jurisdiction). Otherwise a spec could pair
  "gh" with an attacker remote (leaking the GitHub token as Basic Auth) or
  "entire" with an arbitrary token_url (leaking the subject token).

Correctness / perf (Medium):
- collector.go: copy the rolling-window slice headers under the mutex and
  concatenate after unlocking, so the once-per-second snapshot no longer blocks
  concurrent OnSample calls and depresses measured throughput.
- collector.go: drop warm-up samples (Sample.Offset < warmup) so live counts,
  rolling percentiles, and the persisted series match the authoritative level
  result, which excludes warm-up.
- runmgr.go: reset collectors and advance the level index atomically under
  r.mu, and hold r.mu across emitBucket, so a bucket tick during a level
  transition can't attribute the previous level's samples to the new index.
- bench.StartBarrier + RunLevel: build all agents first, then release every
  target together, so target-dependent setup time no longer shifts the
  measured windows and the level-aligned comparison holds. The barrier
  tolerates a target that fails during setup (it still arrives).

Tests: origin guard, secret-source audience, and the existing suite pass under
`go test -race`; lint clean; verified live with a 2-target, 2-level demo run.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
